system.summary: Stager route cipher: words written in columns and copied by a route set by an indicator word, with printed code words (two per meaning, meanings filled in by hand for each issue) for names, places, punctuation and common words, and padding words at the end.
system.notes: The ledgers record the telegrams with the route already undone, so only the code layer is open. Entries counts the Book #1 vocabulary rows of copy mssEC 43 (key_book1_mssEC43.tsv). Each meaning has two code words (left and right printed word): homophones in that sense. Units: the ledger text is words (code words among clear words); length unit "mixed".

prior_solution.where: Decoded at the time; many of the telegrams are printed in clear in the Official Records. No modern decoding of the ledgers' code layer published (Decoding the Civil War phase 3 not reported; searched 27 Oct 2026).

solution.what: Searched for a Decoding the Civil War decipherment phase, a code-word glossary or a data export: none published.
Huntington Digital Library collection p16003coll11: 67 Eckert items, page records carry the volunteers' transcriptions; harvested through the dmwebservices API.
Ledgers hold the telegrams with the route undone and the code words in place, so only the code layer is open.
Cipher Book #1 copies mssEC 41-45 checked against the Feb 1862 ledger mssEC 15: same printed words, different meanings (Andes = Fort Donelson in the book, McClellan in 1862).
mssEC 37, 38, 40 checked for the 1862 filling: post-1866 codes and Banks's 1863 Gulf issue.
Official Records as external plaintext for the 1862 code words (Lander 6 Feb 1862): OR texts not reachable from archive.org full text or eHistory on this machine.
Cipher Book #1, copy mssEC 43, transcribed whole by a subagent (427 vocabulary rows, routes, time code, numerals); page 16 spot-checked against the image.
Book #1 applied to every coded ledger: fits mssEC 25 (Fort Monroe 1864-65; 19.4% of words are book code words) and mssEC 20 (1865-67); Received ledgers are already clear (about 1% false hits).

WAINUT contribution: page records of mssEC 19 (item 9302, War Department Ciphers Sent 1864) and of Cipher Book No. 9 (mssEC 67, item 1750) fetched through the Huntington CONTENTdm API and IIIF images.

WAINUT contribution: Cipher Book No. 9 (mssEC 67; printed also in Plum 1882, vol. 1 appendix) applied to mssEC 19 pp. 1-7: every code word of 11 of the 14 telegrams has a meaning and the telegrams read as sentences (Pagan = Washington, Applause/Abortion = Halleck, Relay = Cavalry, Youth/Yoke = Troops). Book #1 gives other meanings for the same words (Pagan = Battery, Applause = Big Sandy).

WAINUT contribution: second agent re-read every code word used from the No. 9 book images (canvases 1719-1744) and the ledger pp. 1, 3 and 4 from the page images; own decoder, same readings; corrected T6 to Vermont (Brig. Gen.), confirmed Hammer = Fort Monroe (Forts heading, canvas 1735), Palate = Yorktown and Antwerp = Adjutant General (canvas 1729).

WAINUT contribution: OR Ser. I vols. 32 pt. 2 and 33 (archive.org OCR) print T2 and T4-T11 in clear, so 9 of the 11 decoded telegrams are earlier solutions; T1 (Rucker) and T3 (J. H. Taylor) not found there.

WAINUT contribution, in review: D. H. Bates, Lincoln in the Telegraph Office (1907; archive.org cu31924032766846, OCR) searched for T1, T3 and Cipher No. 9: T1 and T3 not in it; No. 9 not discussed (twelve editions described in general, with a No. 12 example and a pointer to Plum).

WAINUT contribution: decode_book9.py --controls (decoded/mssEC19_p1-7_controls.txt): for 64 of 68 code-word tokens of the nine printed telegrams the meaning appears in the printed text of the same telegram (misses: rank words); meanings shuffled among the code words, 500 runs: 4-24 (median 14). Time words match the printed time in 6 of 8.

WAINUT contribution: No. 9 tried on the other three telegrams of pp. 1-7 (U1 Caldwell to Nestor, U2 to Beckwith, U3 prisoners via Cleveland): the meanings give no sense (Midas = New York, Bermuda = F. Sigel, Quarrel = Pemberton; Pauline and Unity blank); another word list probably used.
WAINUT contribution: T1-T11 written as sentences (reading/mssEC19_p1-7.md), read_share 1.0 (v10_relabel.py); U1-U3 kept as a decode, not read (decoded/mssEC19_p1-7_U1-U3_unread.txt).

William Echols (issue #352) matched ledger telegrams of 6-16 Feb 1862 to the printed texts in the Official Records, series I, vol. VII, and read two McClellan to Halleck telegrams of 14 Feb 1862; eleven code words of the February 1862 filling result (key_1862_echols.tsv). Project check: his transcription agrees with transcription/mssEC15.txt, and the values read as sense on pp. 26-28 with the parallel telegrams to Buell and Halleck decoding alike. The printed pages were not checked.

texts.label: mssEC 19 pp. 1-7, telegrams T1-T11 (27 Jan - 5 Feb 1864), decoded with Cipher Book No. 9 (WAINUT)
texts.summary: Halleck's War Department telegrams of late January and early February 1864: Ewell's brigades leaving for Johnston or Longstreet, Johnston's detachment against Sherman's movements in Mississippi, troops and cavalry sent to Harper's Ferry and West Virginia against Early's raid, and Butler left free to relieve North Carolina; plus two staff telegrams to Fort Monroe (Baker's cavalry to Yorktown; Parker's cavalry and recruits from Maine) not found in print.
texts.note: Contributed by WAINUT (27 Oct 2026). This entry covers T1-T11 only, which read whole; the document mssEC19-p1-7 as a whole is read in part, because U1-U3 (next entry) are not read: 11 of its 14 telegrams. read_share measured with research/reading_audit/v10_relabel.py (665 words, no holes). Reading grade left to a reviewer. The contemporary slot holds the OR clear texts of T2 and T4-T11, so 9 of the 11 telegrams are earlier solutions; the new step is tying Cipher Book No. 9 to mssEC 19.
